::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

Falling raindrops are never tear-shaped. Air pressure flattens the base, and past a few millimetres it bursts them.
:::

## Two competing forces

In Earth's atmosphere, a falling droplet experiences two competing forces:
1. **Cohesive Surface Tension Force** ($\propto \gamma d$), which acts to restore spherical symmetry.
2. **Dynamic Aerodynamic Pressure** ($q = \frac{1}{2}\rho_a v^2$), which deforms the droplet's windward face.

Contrary to common illustrations, falling raindrops are never tear-shaped. Their geometry evolves systematically across size regimes.

## Shape regimes by diameter

| Droplet Diameter ($d$) | Terminal Velocity ($v_\infty$) | Dominant Physics | Observed Morphology |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **$< 1.0\text{ mm}$** | $0.5 - 4.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ | Surface tension dominates over dynamic drag | Near-perfect sphere |
| **$1.0 - 4.0\text{ mm}$** | $4.0 - 8.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ | Stagnation pressure at base flattens bottom profile | Oblate spheroid ("hamburger bun") |
| **$4.0 - 6.0\text{ mm}$** | $8.5 - 9.2\text{ m s}^{-1}$ | Aerodynamic shear hollows the droplet center | Inverted parachute / concave base |
| **$> 6.0\text{ mm}$** | $> 9.2\text{ m s}^{-1}$ | Aerodynamic stress exceeds capillary restoring force | Hydrodynamic breakup (Rayleigh-Taylor instability) |

## The Weber number

The transition to instability is characterized by the dimensionless **Weber number** ($We$):

$$We = \frac{\rho_a v_{\infty}^2 d}{\gamma}$$

where:

- $\rho_a$ is the ambient air density ($1.225\text{ kg m}^{-3}$ at sea level).
- $v_\infty$ is the droplet terminal velocity ($\text{m s}^{-1}$).
- $d$ is the equivalent droplet diameter ($\text{m}$).
- $\gamma$ is the surface tension ($\text{N m}^{-1}$).

```{=html}
<figure markdown="span">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 600 330" style="width:100%;max-width:600px;height:auto;font-family:system-ui,-apple-system,sans-serif;" role="img" aria-label="Pressure field around a falling raindrop: high stagnation pressure beneath the base pushes upward while low pressure over the shoulders pulls outward, flattening the drop.">
  <defs>

      <polygon points="0 0, 9 3.5, 0 7" fill="var(--ink-rust)"/>

  <path d="M 338 116 q 10 -26 14 -44" fill="none" stroke="var(--ink-indigo)" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#wdout)"/>
  <text x="300" y="52" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--ink-indigo)" font-size="14.5" font-weight="600">Suction zone — low pressure</text>
  <text x="300" y="72" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--md-default-fg-color--light)" font-size="12.5">flow accelerates over the shoulders, pulling the drop outward</text>
  <line x1="248" y1="248" x2="248" y2="206" stroke="var(--ink-rust)" stroke-width="2.6" marker-end="url(#wdup)"/>
  <line x1="300" y1="256" x2="300" y2="212" stroke="var(--ink-rust)" stroke-width="2.6" marker-end="url(#wdup)"/>
  <line x1="352" y1="248" x2="352" y2="206" stroke="var(--ink-rust)" stroke-width="2.6" marker-end="url(#wdup)"/>
  <text x="300" y="286" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--ink-rust)" font-size="14.5" font-weight="600">Stagnation zone — high pressure</text>
  <text x="300" y="306" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--md-default-fg-color--light)" font-size="12.5">relative updraft decelerates against the base, flattening it</text>
  <path d="M 470 196 q -40 6 -78 -4" fill="none" stroke="var(--md-default-fg-color--light)" stroke-width="1.4" marker-end="url(#wdlead)"/>
  <text x="476" y="192" fill="var(--md-default-fg-color)" font-size="13">flattened underside</text>
  <text x="476" y="210" fill="var(--md-default-fg-color--light)" font-size="12.5">not a teardrop</text>
  <text x="70" y="196" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--md-default-fg-color--light)" font-size="13">We ≈ 12</text>
  <text x="70" y="214" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--md-default-fg-color--light)" font-size="12.5">at rupture</text>
</svg>
<figcaption><strong>Figure 2 | Deformation is the visible result of a pressure difference, not of falling motion.</strong> As the drop falls, air decelerating against its underside raises the local stagnation pressure (magenta, upward), while flow accelerating over the shoulders lowers the pressure there (blue, outward). Surface tension resists both, and the equilibrium shape is wherever the two balance — an oblate spheroid with a flattened, never pointed, base. The Weber number $We = \rho_a v_\infty^2 d / \gamma$ is exactly the ratio of that aerodynamic stress to the capillary restoring stress; once $We \gtrsim 12$ no equilibrium shape exists and the drop enters bag breakup.</figcaption>
</figure>
```


When $We \gtrsim 12$, dynamic pressure hollows the droplet out into a thin liquid bag surrounded by a thicker toroidal rim. Within milliseconds, the central bag bursts into a fine mist of micro-droplets, while the toroidal rim fragments via capillary Plateau-Rayleigh instability into larger satellite drops. This imposes a strict natural upper limit on atmospheric raindrops of approximately $5\text{ to }6\text{ mm}$.

## Key takeaways

- A falling drop is shaped by surface tension pulling it spherical against dynamic pressure $\tfrac{1}{2}\rho_a v^2$ flattening its underside; it is never tear-shaped.
- Below $1\text{ mm}$ the drop is a sphere; from $1$ to $4\text{ mm}$ it is an oblate "hamburger bun"; between $4$ and $6\text{ mm}$ the base hollows into an inverted parachute.
- The Weber number $We = \rho_a v_\infty^2 d/\gamma$ is the ratio of aerodynamic stress to capillary stress; past $We \approx 12$ no equilibrium shape exists.
- Bag breakup caps natural raindrops at roughly $5$ to $6\text{ mm}$: the thin bag bursts into mist and the rim fragments into satellite drops.
